title: The parish
hook: the local family of the Church

segments.voice: Yesterday, secular institutes: vows lived in ordinary jobs, like leaven in the dough. Your line was hidden in the world. Which ordinary task did you do as a quiet prayer? Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

Here's a small surprise for anyone who has moved house. When a Catholic settles into a new address, Church law gives them a new parish along with it, before any registration form is filled in. The law draws parishes, as a general rule, by territory, so the street you sleep on decides which parish is yours. The church down the road may have a bingo night, a youth group with a broken ping-pong table, and a priest who still hasn't learned your name. It's yours anyway. Today, the parish.
screen: `THE BOXES ARE STILL TAPED SHUT.` → `THE STREET DECIDES THE PARISH.` → `IT'S YOURS ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: First, what a parish is. The word often gets used for the building, the brick church with the parking lot. The Code of Canon Law describes something else: a community of the Christian faithful, set up for good, within a particular church, whose pastoral care is entrusted to a pastor under the authority of the bishop. A community first. The building is where that community gathers. Second, how you belong. The Code says that, as a general rule, a parish is territorial. It takes in all the faithful who live within its borders. There are also personal parishes, formed around a rite, a language or a nationality, so a Spanish-speaking or Vietnamese-speaking community may have a parish that crosses the map. But the default is simple: you belong where you live. Third, what happens there. The Book of Acts describes the first believers in Jerusalem this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." Teaching, the breaking of bread, prayer. A parish is where those three things happen within walking or driving distance of your front door: baptisms and funerals, confessions on Saturday, the Sunday Mass, a food pantry in the basement. Last, why it matters on a Tuesday. A parish is not chosen for its music or its preacher, though some people do shop around. It's given, like a family. That means sharing a pew with people you didn't pick, and that is part of what makes it a family.
screen: `A COMMUNITY BEFORE A BUILDING.` · `YOU BELONG WHERE YOU LIVE.` · `TEACHING, BREAD AND PRAYER.` · `GIVEN, LIKE A FAMILY.` · then, large: `THE BREAKING OF BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two parts. First, now: settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the parish nearest where you live, whether you go there or not. Picture its doors, its steps, the people who come and go. If you pray, you can pray for the people inside it this week, by name if you know any. If you don't pray, hold them in mind with a little goodwill. Second, later: if you go to Mass this week, introduce yourself to one person you've seen but never met. A name is enough. The bell holds the time.
Parish. The local family of the Church: a community of the faithful, usually drawn by where they live, cared for by a pastor under the bishop. Today's word.
Your line: home base. Today, find out which parish your street belongs to, and walk or drive past it once, just to see its doors. Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Catholics normally belong to the parish where they live, and register there for the sacraments and parish life. Personal parishes also serve people of a particular rite, language or nationality.

notes: Editor pass: hook no longer claims a Catholic 'has usually already changed parishes' with 'no form'; now says Church law gives a new parish with a settled address, before any registration form. Carry no longer asks for the parish's patron saint, since day 1414's practice is learning the diocese's patron.

Canon 515 §1 (definition of a parish), canon 518 (generally territorial; personal parishes by rite, language, nationality or other reason), canon 519 (pastor under the authority of the diocesan bishop) paraphrased: confirm.

Hook says a Catholic 'has usually already changed parishes' on moving, without registration: canonically true by domicile/quasi-domicile (canon 102, 107), though US parishes commonly ask people to register. A Keeper may want this softened.
Spanish- and Vietnamese-speaking communities are illustrative examples of personal parishes by language; confirm acceptable.
The parish etymology (Greek paroikia) is deliberately left out under the claims rule.
